We identified 209 youth aged 8-11 years who reported NSSI at Y2, but not at baseline (incident NSSI; iNSSI) and 209 controls matched by demographic and clinical characteristics. We conducted a Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regularization, which yielded an AUC of .60, to narrow down predictors for logistic regression. Significant main effects indicated that lower GFA of the left parolfactory section of the cingulum (OR���=���0.63) and higher negative urgency (OR���=���1.54) were prospectively associated with Y2 NSSI. Sex interactions indicated that the relations between Y2 NSSI and lower GFA of the left parolfactory section of the cingulum (OR���=���1.75) and higher negative urgency (OR���=���0.60) were driven by males. Higher sensation seeking (OR���=���1.36) and lack of perseverance (OR���=���1.46) were more strongly associated with Y2 NSSI among females than males. Future work is needed to better understand the course of development of white matter microstructure and impulsivity as it relates to NSSI.

Overwhelming evidence found that adolescents with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) exhibit structural brain alterations. The influence of mTBI on the adolescents' structural covariance networks (SCNs) remains unexplored. In this study, data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study were adopted, comprising 450 adolescents with mTBI and 450 matched controls for clinical behavior analysis. After structural magnetic resonance imaging��quality control, 415 adolescents with mTBI and 404 matched controls were finally included in the SCNs analysis. The SCNs were established using cortical thickness (CT) and cortical surface area (CSA), with group differences assessed via nonparametric permutation tests. The results demonstrated that adolescents with mTBI suffered from impaired cognitive function, including worse working memory, processing speed, and sleep quality. Furthermore, adolescents with mTBI demonstrated both reduced CSA and CT in the��executive control network (ECN), including the superior parietal lobule, anterior cingulate cortex, superior frontal gyrus, and insula. In addition, network nodal metrics in these regions also showed abnormalities. These findings might suggest that impaired executive function is associated with aberrant SCNs of hubs in ECN in adolescents with mTBI.

Childhood irritability and negative life events have been linked to internalizing symptoms; however, it remains unclear how these factors jointly shape symptom trajectories. We examined independent and interactive effects of irritability and negative life events on the development of depressive, anxiety, and somatic symptoms. Participants included 9- to 10-year-old children (N���=���11,868) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (ABCD Study�). Linear mixed-effects modeling was utilized to investigate the longitudinal trajectories of depressive, anxiety, and somatic symptoms across three annual follow-up assessments, with irritability, including both tonic and phasic irritability, negative life events, and their interaction included as predictors. Higher irritability and greater exposure to negative life events independently predicted changes in depressive, anxiety, and somatic symptom trajectories over time. Irritability and negative life events also interacted to predict depressive symptom trajectories, with greater negative life event exposure amplifying differences in depressive symptom trajectories across irritability levels. Similar patterns were observed for tonic and phasic irritability. No significant interactions were observed for anxiety or somatic symptom trajectories. Irritability and negative life events independently contribute to multiple domains of internalizing psychopathology, but their joint effects appear to be specific to depressive symptom development.

Traumatic stress exposure is a risk factor for greater drug use variety, but there remains limited research on peer mediators of this relationship. This study sought to examine traumatic stress exposure as a predictor of drug use variety and determine whether peer drug use and/or peer drug selling/gifting significantly mediate this relationship. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development dataset was analyzed. The first four waves were used. Generalized structural equation modeling was used to estimate direct and indirect relationships of interest. Past year traumatic stress exposure prior to Wave 2 was associated with greater drug use variety at Wave 4. Greater peer drug selling/gifting and peer drug use scores at Wave 3 also predicted significantly greater drug use variety at Wave 4. However, only peer drug use significantly mediated the relationship between traumatic stress exposure and drug use variety. Traumatic stress exposure early in life may be associated with greater risk for greater drug use variety. Peer drug use behaviors among those who have experienced trauma should be targeted for intervention as a means of mitigating this risk.

Previous research has shown that gender minorities face health inequities, including mental and physical health disparities, but few studies have examined cardiovascular disparities, such as lipid profiles, in early adolescents. Monitoring cholesterol in adolescence is important, as early lipid levels can predict future cardiovascular risk. This study aimed to assess associations between multiple measures of gender diversity and cholesterol profiles among early adolescents. Data from 1511 participants aged 10-14 years in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (2018-2021) were analyzed. Gender diversity was measured using transgender identity, felt gender (how much one feels like a boy/girl), gender expression (how gender is communicated through appearance and mannerisms), and gender non-contentedness (desire to be a sex or gender different from sex assigned at birth). Cholesterol measures included total, high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and non-HDL cholesterol. Multivariable linear and modified Poisson regression models adjusted for sociodemographic factors were used to estimate associations. Participants were 47.0% female, 37.9% racial and ethnic minority, and 1.9-19.1% were gender-diverse depending on the measure. Higher felt gender and gender non-contentedness scores were associated with lower HDL cholesterol. Gender non-contentedness was associated with higher non-HDL cholesterol. Some measures of gender diversity were associated with less favorable lipid profiles, including reduced HDL cholesterol. These findings build on prior research examining cardiovascular health in gender-diverse populations and highlight the need to investigate mechanisms underlying these associations.

Abnormalities in reward sensitivity and cognitive control are observed in multiple psychiatric disorders. However, differences in measurement of reward sensitivity and cognitive control across studies have yielded mixed findings. Despite assumptions of convergence, the correlation between survey-based and task-based assessments of these constructs remains small. In this preregistered study of data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study (N = 11,875; ages 9-12 years), we examined relationships across these constructs and with psychopathology using exploratory structural equation modelling. We found evidence for multiple cognitive control and reward sensitivity factors with modest correlations. Cognitive control and reward sensitivity independently related to both Internalizing and Externalizing psychopathology factors two years later (�? = 0.01 to |0.605|). Our findings highlight the utility of using multiple methods and raters to capture variance in reward sensitivity and cognitive control, showing they are multidimensional constructs each with unique relationships to psychopathology in adolescence.

Despite growing recognition of cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS), the developmental mechanisms linking early adversity to CDS symptoms remain largely unknown. This study addresses this gap by examining whether executive function (EF) serves as a cognitive mechanism linking cumulative adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) to later CDS symptoms and whether this mediational chain differs by adolescent sex. Data were drawn from the prospective longitudinal Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study�. The final analytic sample included 4,678 adolescents (52.5% male) identifying primarily as White (72.5%), Hispanic/Latino (13.6%), and Black (13.1%). A moderated mediation model was tested using cumulative ACEs score (ages 9-11) as the predictor, EF deficits (ages 12-13) as the mediator, CDS symptoms (ages 13-14) as the outcome, and adolescent sex as moderator. Results indicate cumulative ACEs predict later CDS symptoms above and beyond baseline levels. EF deficits partially mediated the ACEs-CDS link (accounting for 30% of the effect). Notably, adolescent sex moderated the EF-CDS pathway; while adversity impacted EF similarly across sexes, the association between EF deficits and CDS symptoms was significantly stronger for female adolescents. These findings provide the first prospective evidence that early adversity accelerates CDS development via disruptions in executive functioning. The results support a developmental psychopathology model of CDS and identify EF as a potentially modifiable intervention target, particularly for female adolescents exposed to early adversity.

Early motor and language milestones are key indicators of neurodevelopment, yet their associations with later autism traits and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms remain poorly understood. Neurobiological mechanisms linking early developmental delays to these conditions are not well established. Here, we investigate associations between early developmental milestones, resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC), and neurodevelopmental traits in a large adolescent sample. Data were drawn from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (ABCD) and included 6,663 participants (age range��=��8.92-11.08��years; mean age��=��9.92��years; 48.42% female). Developmental measures included roll over, sit without assistance, walk without assistance, speech development, gross motor development, and coordination. Autism traits were assessed using the Social Responsiveness Scale, and ADHD symptoms were assessed using the Attention Problems subscale of the Child Behavior Checklist. rsFC was examined within and between cortical and subcortical regions. Linear mixed-effects (LME) models and Bayesian mediation analyses assessed associations between developmental measures, rsFC, and neurodevelopmental traits. LME models revealed shared and condition-specific associations. Poor coordination was associated with higher autism traits and ADHD symptoms, whereas delayed speech development was associated with autism traits, and delayed walking without assistance with ADHD symptoms. We found negligible evidence that rsFC measures mediated associations between early developmental milestones and neurodevelopmental traits. Indirect effects were modest, accounting for less than 2% of associations with autism traits, although somewhat larger effects were observed for ADHD symptoms. These findings suggest overlapping developmental pathways, with intrinsic connectivity reflecting downstream neural processes rather than primary mediating mechanisms.

Adolescence is a critical developmental stage, and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are important environmental factors influencing behavior. However, the relationship between ACEs, individual behavior, brain mechanisms, and the role of genetic risk remains underexplored. In this study, data from 9796 youths aged 9-13 years in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study were analyzed, including 67 ACE-related variables and 30 behavioral outcomes. Using sparse canonical correlation analysis, we identified two distinct patterns: a parental mental health-child psychopathology, linking parental psychiatric status to child mental health (r���=���0.576, Pperm < 0.001) and a socioeconomic-cognitive development, in which higher family socioeconomic status and a more supportive family atmosphere correlated with better child cognition (r���=���-0.272, Pperm < 0.008). Neuroimaging revealed these associations were mediated by structural alterations in brain regions including the temporal and parietal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellar cortex, along with changes in white matter tracts and functional networks. Genetic risk for psychiatric disorders significantly moderated these ACEs-brain-behavior pathways, with effects varying across ancestry groups. Longitudinal cross-lagged panel models further demonstrated that parental psychiatric conditions, particularly depression and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, predicted child psychiatric symptoms two years later. Our findings delineate distinct ACEs-related pathways influencing adolescent behavior through neurostructural and functional mediators, moderated by genetic risk. This integrated framework advances the understanding of ACEs mechanisms and highlights targets for early intervention.

To determine the relative impact of multilevel protective factors on co-occurring pain, psychological, and somatic symptom (co-PPSS) trajectories from late childhood through early adolescence. We conducted secondary analyses of longitudinal Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study data collected from 2016 to 2023. Youth were classified into asymptomatic, low/stable, moderate/persistent, and high/worsening co-PPSS trajectories derived from annual parent-reported symptom data. Child (coping skills), family (parental wellbeing, parental acceptance, family harmony), and peer-level (peer acceptance, prosocial behavior) protective factors were assessed across years using youth- and parent-reported surveys. Multinomial logistic regression examined the association of these factors with risk of higher co-PPSS trajectories. We report standardized adjusted relative risk ratios (adj.RRR) with 95% confidence intervals ([CIs]). We included data from 8,817 youth (aged 9.92�0.63 yrs. at baseline, 14.08�0.68 at year five), 2,270 (25.8%) and 677 (7.7%) of whom were classified with moderate/persistent or high/worsening co-PPSS trajectories. Apart from parental wellbeing and prosocial behavior, each protective factor was associated with a reduced relative risk for a high/worsening and moderate/persistent trajectory. Higher parental acceptance was associated with a 28% (RRR 0.72 [CI 0.66, 0.79]) and 15% (RRR 0.85 [CI 0.80, 0.92]) reduced relative risk for a high/worsening and moderate/persistent co-PPSS trajectory, respectively. High (vs. low) peer acceptance was also associated with reduced relative risk for the high/worsening (RRR 0.34 [0.27, 0.42]) and moderate/persistent (RRR 0.48 [0.40, 0.56]) trajectories. Findings underscore the potential importance of enhancing youths' family support, coping, and positive peer relationships to co-PPSS resilience.

Irritability is associated with an array of deleterious outcomes, yet research examining developmental antecedents is limited. The present study addresses this gap by examining cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control as predictors of irritability from late childhood through early adolescence. A second-order latent growth curve model (LGCM) was constructed to investigate irritability across ages 9-13 using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study (N =���11,720, 47.9% female). Cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control were examined as predictors. Sensitivity analyses controlled for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms, defiance, and biological sex. The best-fitting unconditional LGCM showed a modest but significant linear decline in irritability from late childhood through early adolescence, with significant inter-individual variability. In conditional LGCMs, lower levels of cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control at baseline predicted higher levels of irritability at baseline and a faster decline in irritability over time. The effects of cognitive variables on irritability trajectories were attenuated to non-significance when ADHD symptoms, defiance, and biological sex were included as covariates. Using a large, nationally representative sample, this study characterizes the average trajectory of irritability from late childhood through early adolescence. Results suggest that while there appears to be a concurrent effect of cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control on irritability, this may diminish over time. Moreover, ADHD symptoms, defiance, and biological sex may play a more central role. Future research should investigate these associations under frustration, when cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control are key.

Racial-ethnically minoritized youth are at elevated risk for early substance use (SU; typically defined as occurring before age 15). Research rarely investigates how different forms of discrimination, such as racial-ethnic and weight discrimination, may operate differently by sex. The current study investigated how these two forms of discrimination differentially relate to early SU, assessed subjectively and objectively, among racial-ethnically minoritized boys and girls. Data were drawn from 571���U.S. racial-ethnically minoritized youth (51% female; Mage=11.75 years old) in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, which began in 2016-18. Main exposure variables included racial-ethnic and weight discrimination. Main outcomes included self-reported SU over the past year and hair sample-based SU over the past three months. Sociodemographic and psychosocial covariates that may be related to SU were included. Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses were conducted, separately by sex assigned at birth. Logistic regression-based path analysis (accounting for non-independence) revealed sex-specific patterns. Among racial-ethnically minoritized boys, racial-ethnic discrimination was associated with increased likelihood of self-reported early SU concurrently (OR = 1.42; 95%CI = [1.19, 1.71]). Among racial-ethnically minoritized girls, weight discrimination was associated with increased likelihood of hair sample-based early SU concurrently (OR = 3.48; 95% CI = [1.37, 8.83]) and one year later (OR = 3.61; 95% CI = [1.07, 12.23]). This study underscores the unique influences of racial-ethnic and weight discrimination faced by racial-ethnically minoritized boys and girls, separately. Results highlight the need for programs and practices to address these unique experiences to effectively prevent early SU.

Refinement of large-scale functional networks during adolescence facilitates maturation of cognitive and affective functions vital to adult wellbeing, including working memory and emotion regulation. Understanding how functional connectivity (FC) subserves these abilities can offer valuable insight into typical neurodevelopment and brain-based markers of vulnerability to psychopathology. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study includes a task designed to engage both working memory and affective processing: the Emotional N-back (EN-back). This study applied connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) to baseline EN-back fMRI data (n���=���4326) to examine whole-brain FC patterns underlying EN-back performance. Separate models were run to predict overall and stimulus-specific accuracy (i.e., places, happy, fearful, and neutral faces). To probe neurodevelopmental change, CPM was applied to N-back fMRI data among adults in the Human Connectome Project (HCP; n���=���515). CPM identified networks predictive of overall task performance (Total-accuracy) and all stimuli (rho = 0.26 - 0.35, p���<���.001) in ABCD. Total-accuracy network strength was a significant predictor of externalizing problems (�? = -0.002, t���=���-5.06, p���=���0.0000004), and generalized to predict task performance across brain states (resting-state: rho = 0.13, p���<���.001) and time (2-year follow-up: rho = 0.37, p���<���.005). CPM also identified a network predictive of Total N-back accuracy among adult HCP participants (rho = 0.48, p���<���.05), characterized by common and distinct FC patterns. This work provides novel insight into whole-brain mechanisms of EN-back performance at the onset of adolescence and patterns of neurodevelopment from early adolescence to adulthood.

Early puberty timing is linked to altered neurodevelopment and adverse mental health outcomes, yet its relationship with cognitive functioning remains unclear. We examined the effects of puberty timing across multiple cognitive domains. In 10,722 participants from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, we assessed associations between puberty timing, operationalized using sex specific logistic growth curve models, and performance on six cognitive tasks at baseline, 2-year, and 4-year follow-ups. Linear-mixed regression models were calculated separately by sex, adjusting for age, bodyweight, parental income, race/ethnicity, birthweight, prenatal alcohol/tobacco exposure, and whether the assessment occurred before or after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. To probe causal relationships, we performed Mendelian randomization utilizing external Genome Wide Association Study (GWAS) data on age at menarche (N���=���632,955), male puberty timing (N���=���205,354), and executive functioning (N���=���427,037). In the ABCD study, earlier puberty timing was associated with poorer performance pooled across timepoints on the NIH Toolbox� Picture Sequence Memory Task (girls: standardized �?���=���.04, 95% CI [0.02, 0.06]; boys: �?���=���.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.06]), the learning of a word list (girls: �?���=���.05, 95% CI [0.02, 0.08]; boys: �?���=���.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.05]), and NIH Toolbox� List Sorting Task (boys only: boys: �?���=���.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.06]). Mendelian randomization indicated better executive functioning with later age at menarche (b���=���0.005/year, 95% CI [0.000, 0.011]). The association with male puberty timing was directionally consistent but remained nonsignificant (b���=���0.012/year, 95% CI [-0.004, 0.028]). These findings suggest a causal link between earlier puberty timing and poorer cognitive performance. However, effect sizes were small, indicating limited clinical implications at the individual level, while potentially remaining relevant at the population level. Future research on atypical pubertal development or medically induced puberty suppression should include assessment of cognitive outcomes.

Cannabis use during early adolescence can negatively affect brain development and increase the risk of adverse health. We aimed to examine trends and correlates of cannabis-use susceptibility, a psychosocial receptivity construct capturing openness to future use (i.e., absence of a firm commitment not to use, curiosity, and willingness to try if offered) among youth who have not initiated cannabis. This study analyzed five waves of the adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) study (11,868 unique participants; n = 33,181 person-wave observations) to estimate the prevalence of cannabis-use susceptibility from late childhood (ages 9-10, baseline) through early adolescence (ages 13-14, 4-year follow-up). We fit wave-specific weighted multivariable logistic regression models and a pooled generalized estimating equations logistic model across all five waves to examine associations of individual, non-cannabis substance use, psychosocial factors, family, school, and neighborhood environmental factors with cannabis-use susceptibility. Among never-cannabis users, the prevalence of cannabis-use susceptibility increased from 5.8% at baseline (ages: 9-10 years) to 22.7% at the 4-year follow-up (aged:13-14 years). In the pooled generalized estimating equation model, later follow-up waves, economic hardship, prior non-cannabis substance use, parental substance use, and several impulsivity-related traits were associated with higher susceptibility. In contrast, higher parental monitoring, a favorable school environment, and positive child-perceived neighborhood safety were associated with lower susceptibility. Wave-specific models showed that the magnitude and statistical significance of some associations varied across developmental stages. This study highlights the influence of behavioral and environmental factors on cannabis-use susceptibility. Early intervention efforts that enhance parental monitoring, school support, and community environments may help reduce risk.

Inhibitory control is a core cognitive function whose competence varies across the population, with impairments often observed in psychiatric conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The Stop Signal Task (SST) is a widely used paradigm for assessing this ability. However, conventional formalizations of SST performance, such as the independent race model, rely on assumptions that are frequently violated in modern experimental designs. Furthermore, they typically fit only mean reaction times, overlooking crucial trial-by-trial dynamics. To address these limitations, we formalize the SST as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). This framework characterizes inhibitory control with two components: noisy perceptual inference regarding stimuli and optimal control balanced against potential costs. To fit this model to the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study baseline cohort (N���=���3,567), we introduce Transformer-encoded Simulation-Based Inference (TeSBI). This end-to-end architecture learns compact, sequence-aware embeddings from raw behavioral data. It enables efficient, amortized inference of individual-level posteriors. Extensive validation confirms it extracts reliable and identifiable parameters. We identify distinct latent computational attributes associated with scores on ADHD questionnaires. Controlling for sex, IQ, and medication status, children with higher ADHD scores exhibit subtle but robust shifts in computational attributes. They show a reduction in go cue directional precision, alongside a blunted sensitivity to stop error, go error and time costs. The learned embedding space reveals a continuous manifold in which children with higher ADHD scores are heterogeneously distributed, rather than forming distinct disorder clusters. This indicates that similar clinical characteristics can emerge from diverse combinations of computational mechanisms, supporting a dimensional perspective on neurodiversity. Our end-to-end framework can be extended to a broader range of cognitive tasks. It offers a scalable, theory-driven solution for analyzing large-scale behavioral data.

Household and neighborhood socioeconomic status (SES) have consistently been associated with both brain structure and functional connectivity in adolescence. However, there is considerable heterogeneity in brain outcomes among youth from disadvantaged backgrounds, which suggests that other factors-including aspects of one's lifestyle-likely play a role by moderating these associations. In a large sample of ~10,000 early adolescents from the baseline assessment of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (aged 9-10 years), we tested whether sleep and participation in physical and non-physical extracurricular activities moderate associations of household and neighborhood disadvantage with brain structure and functional connectivity. Higher sleep duration was linked to weaker associations between both household and neighborhood disadvantage and a range of structural and functional brain measures, whereas extracurricular engagement had more selective moderating effects on the structure of sensory regions. Our findings identify sleep duration and extracurricular engagement as markers of variability in SES-brain associations, underscoring the need for longitudinal and intervention studies to determine whether these factors can mitigate disparities in brain outcomes among youth from disadvantaged backgrounds.

Most longitudinal studies lack multi-wave measures and rarely consider cognitive mechanisms, such as cognitive control, that may shape both the development of mental health and social media use. This study examined dynamic within-person relations and stable between-person correlations linking social media browsing (SMB), overall screen time, cognitive control, and depressive and anxiety symptoms across early- to mid-adolescence. Participants were from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (N = 9,747, 52.3% female) assessed at baseline, 2-year, and 4-year follow-ups. Primary measures included self-reported SMB and overall screen time, parent-reported depressive and anxiety symptoms, and performance-based cognitive control from the Flanker and Stop Signal tasks. Random intercept cross-lagged panel models estimated within-person time-lagged associations and between-person correlations. Gender was examined as a moderator. The within-person results revealed a cognitive pathway across genders and screen time types. When adolescents increased SMB (and overall screen time) at baseline, this predicted reduced cognitive control 2 years later (�? = -.06, p = .020), which in turn predicted increased depressive symptoms at the 4-year follow-up (�? = -.06, p = .010). Additionally, females with more baseline screen time had increased depressive symptoms 2 years later (�? = .05, p = .016), which subsequently predicted increased screen time and anxiety symptoms at the 4-year follow-up (�?s = .09 to .13, p's < .050). Reduced cognitive control may be a general mechanism linking adolescent screen use and SMB to later depressive symptoms across genders, whereas changes in affect may be a gender-specific pathway in females.

Adolescence is a critical period of brain development characterized by heightened reward sensitivity, which influences behavior and emotional regulation. Major life events, like the COVID-19 pandemic, may affect reward system development. This longitudinal study integrates self-reported Behavioral Activation System (BAS) measures with fMRI data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study� to examine reward processing during versus before the pandemic. 5,405 participants (Mage = 9.92, SD = 0.62) completed the Monetary Incentive Delay task during fMRI scanning and BAS assessments at Baseline and Year 2. Participants were grouped by whether their Year 2 follow-up occurred before or during the pandemic. Generalized linear mixed models examined changes in BAS subscales (Drive, Fun-Seeking, Reward Responsiveness); fMRI analyses assessed neural activation in key cortical/subcortical regions. Brain network analysis evaluated functional connectivity across reward and executive networks. Results revealed a decline across all BAS subscales at Year 2 compared to Baseline, with more pronounced reductions in BAS Drive among those assessed during the pandemic. Network analysis showed cohesive executive but variable reward network changes, especially in the right hemisphere. Developmental changes in reward sensitivity were accompanied by shifts in activation in core reward regions (e.g., nucleus accumbens, caudate, putamen, thalamus), which also varied by age and sex. Findings show declines in reward sensitivity over time, and reveal subtle but meaningful adaptations in reward-related brain function in relation to the pandemic, highlighting the need to consider individual differences during adolescence, especially under stress.

Engagement in sports is associated with cognitive and academic functioning in youth. However, heterogenous methodology has resulted in mixed findings across the literature. We propose a new method for investigating how sports activity may affect cognition through metabolic equivalents (MET)-minutes per week during sports engagement and compare it against total number of sports engaged. Using the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, 9,973 children between the ages of 9 and 10 years old were included. Parent report of children's engagement in sports over the past year were utilized to calculate total MET-minutes per week. Youth participants completed the National Institutes of Health Toolbox. Generalized Additive Mixed Models were run to examine the relationship between MET-minutes on cognition, while controlling for Body Mass Index. The contribution of MET-minutes compared to total count of sports on cognitive performance were compared using Akaike Information Criterion values. Both total MET-minutes per week and past-year total sports were non-linearly associated with increased performance on multiple tasks of executive functioning and decreased expressive vocabulary. MET-minutes were shown to contribute more robustly to models of cognition than total number of sports. Past year MET-minutes per week was associated with increased cognitive performance, particularly in the domain of executive functioning, and was more sensitive to differences in cognition in contrast to total sports engagement. Indicating that greater measurement sensitivity for physical activity may increase predictive power on cognitive performance outcomes. Our findings provide more support for increasing physical activity in youth to promote cognitive trajectories.

This study investigated the associations between prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE), including low and moderate levels of exposure, and parent-reported sleep disturbances during adolescence. This is an area that remains understudied despite evidence linking PAE, particularly heavy PAE, to poor sleep in younger children and the growing recognition of harms associated with low levels of PAE. Participants were 10,336 adolescents (aged 12-13) from the fourth assessment wave of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. Cross-sectional generalised linear mixed models and generalised additive mixed models were used to assess the impact of prenatal alcohol exposure, conceptualised as the presence or absence of PAE, total drinks consumed during pregnancy (i.e. dose) and patterns of PAE (i.e. abstainers, light reducing, light stable, heavy reducing), on parent-reported adolescent sleep disturbances, while controlling for important birth related, environmental and medical factors. Adolescents with any PAE experienced worse overall parent-reported sleep disturbances compared to those without, with sleep-wake transitions, excessive somnolence and sleep breathing being the domains most impacted. There was limited support for a dose-response relationship between low-level PAE and sleep problems in adolescence. However, those with a pattern of PAE before knowledge of pregnancy, compared to abstainers, experienced greater problems with sleep-wake transitions and sleep breathing. These findings contribute to the growing evidence that there are no safe levels of alcohol consumption during pregnancy, as even low to moderate PAE negatively impacts adolescent sleep. Identifying sleep-wake transitions, excessive somnolence and sleep breathing as the most affected domains provides targets for both screening and intervention.

The endocannabinoid (eCB) system underlies many biological processes and is thought to be critical in adolescent brain development. However, the eCB system's contributions to brain morphometry during adolescence remains understudied. Here we investigated cross-sectional associations between brain structure and circulating eCBs and related lipids in a subsample of adolescents (N = 294, ages 10-14, 44.5% female, 65.3% White) from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) study utilizing a structural equation modeling approach. After accounting for sex and age, significant covariance between circulating eCBs and related lipids and cortical thickness, surface area, and volume in brain regions throughout the cortex were revealed. While the mechanisms underlying these associations need further research, these results suggest that the eCB system likely plays a critical role in early-adolescent brain development. Future work should determine underlying mechanisms, evaluate these associations longitudinally, and consider sex differences and the modulatory effects of pubertal hormones.

Adolescence is a critical developmental period marked by heightened vulnerability to initiating substance use, with long-term implications for health and behavior. Nicotine, alcohol, and cannabis are the most commonly used substances among adolescents. Their use often co-occurs but few studies have described or quantified the patterns and doses of substance co-use in this vulnerable population. We used data from six waves of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study. Substance use was measured through a web-based timeline followback interview, and outcomes are operationalized into substance use quantity (in standard units), single use, and co-use (use of two substances on the same day) of alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine. Group differences of average dose in standard units between single use and co-use for each substance class were analyzed using linear mixed-effects modeling in years 4-6. The average dose of nicotine was significantly higher when co-used with alcohol (4.32; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.55-6.09; p < .001) or when co-used with cannabis (4.41; 95% CI: 2.76-6.05; p < .001) in year 6; nicotine trends were similar in years four and five. In year 6, the average dose of alcohol was higher when co-used with cannabis (1.87; 95% CI: 0.37-3.36; p = .004) or co-used with nicotine (1.64; 95% CI: 0.06-3.22; p = .03) compared to single use of alcohol. The average dose of cannabis was not significantly different when used singularly or co-used with either alcohol or nicotine in our study years. During adolescence, the co-use of substances (namely alcohol and nicotine) may lead to higher average doses compared to single-substance use.

ObjectivePrevious research has yielded mixed findings regarding the validity of the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) DSM-Oriented Scales (DOSs) in identifying DSM diagnoses. The present study evaluates the concurrent validity of the DOSs by comparing scale classifications with a gold-standard clinical interview.MethodsParticipants (N = 11,851) were children in the NIH Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study whose caregivers completed the CBCL and the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (KSADS) semi-structured interview at baseline (9.92 years, SD = 0.63), two-year follow-up (12.03 years, SD = 0.67), or both.Results2,321 (19.59%) children at baseline and 1,708 (15.57%) participants at two-year follow-up met criteria for one or more KSADS disorders. Sensitivity of the CBCL relative to KSADS diagnoses was generally low (10.36% - 75.00%), with only two scales above 50%. Specificity was high (92.47% - 97.07%). Positive predictive values were low (0.71% - 48.20%), and negative predictive values were high (89.84% - 99.90%). Area under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.55 to 0.84.DiscussionIn the present sample, the DOSs showed poor concurrent validity with a gold standard clinical interview. Caution should be exercised when using the CBCL due to the high rates of false negatives.

The dual systems model has risen to prominence as a developmental framework because of its capacity for understanding adolescents' high propensity for risky behaviors during this period of the life-course. While development of impulse control and sensation-seeking mainly occurs during adolescence, childhood and exposures during childhood may lead to long-term impacts on development during this period of the life-course. Sexual abuse in childhood may be a particularly relevant predictor of differential development of these constructs. This study addressed these gaps in the literature by examining sexual abuse as a predictor of differential development of impulse control and sensation-seeking during childhood and early adolescence. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development data were analyzed. Group-based trajectory modeling was used to identify developmental heterogeneity in impulse control and sensation-seeking. Multinomial logistic regression was used to examine sexual abuse variety as a predictor of differential development. Results indicated that a four-group model of impulse control development (High Impulse Control, Moderate Impulse Control, Declining Impulsivity, High Impulsivity) and a three-group model of sensation-seeking development (High Sensation-Seeking, Moderate Sensation-Seeking, Low Sensation-Seeking) best fit the data. Greater sexual abuse variety predicted increased risk of assignment to the High Sensation-Seeking group, but did not predict impulse control development.

In this registered report, we introduce a new discordant sibling random-intercept cross-lagged panel model and apply it to investigate within-person/family and between-family bidirectional associations of parental monitoring-related phenotypes and youth externalizing behaviors. We used data from 1,956 twin/sibling pairs (Mage at first assessment = 10 years; 51% male, 59% White; 14% Black; 15% Hispanic; <1% Asian; 11% Other race/ethnicity) contributing up to six annual waves of data collection from the adolescent brain and cognitive development study, a nationally representative data collection effort including 11,875 children enrolled and assessed across 21 sites across the United States. DS latent curve models with structured residuals models were needed to account for change over time, converged, and fit the data well. We found few within-person/family effects consistent with hypotheses, concentrated from age 13-15 that were likely environmentally mediated. Potentially causal effects within-person/family effects included more youth-reported child disclosure at age 13 predicting lower parent-reported externalizing at age 14, and more youth externalizing problems at age 13 with less monitoring at age 14; other within-person/family associations were driven by familial confounding. Unexpected positive between-family lagged effects in the same developmental window reflect novel family-level processes that may be driven by evocative gene-environment correlations.

Prior literature within the field of human-animal interaction has illuminated the potential impact of companion animals on prosocial behaviors. This study explores pet ownership association with both adolescent self-reported and parent-reported adolescent engagement in prosocial behavior, using a large dataset of adolescents in the United States, collected between the years of 2019-2022. This study analyzes secondary data from the longitudinal ABCD Study. The final analytic sample includes 8504 adolescents (53.4% boys) with an average age of 12.46 (SD���=���0.68) at Time 1 and 13.6 (SD���=���0.73) at Time 2. Ordinal logistic regressions were estimated within a structural equation modeling framework to evaluate if pet ownership type (e.g., dog owners, cat owners) was associated with increased odds of parent- and adolescent-reported engagement in prosocial behaviors as measured by an adapted subscale from the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire controlling for age and gender. The parent-report adolescent prosocial latent variable indicated no significant effect of pet ownership. The adolescent self-report prosocial latent variable revealed that adolescents in dog-owning and mixed-pet (e.g., cats and dogs) households had greater odds of agreeing that they engage in prosocial behavior compared to adolescents in non-pet households. There was a significant interaction between pet ownership and gender, with girls in mixed-pet household having greater odds of reporting prosocial behavior compared to boys in non-pet households. Repeated-measures analysis demonstrated relative stability between the Time 1 and Time 2 waves in terms of broad within-group responses to prosocial behavior items. This research highlights differences between types of pet-owning families in terms of reported engagement in prosocial behaviors.
